## Conclusion

State-funded preschool improves school readiness at kindergarten entry and, where it has been followed far enough, raises high-school and college attainment [6]; it does not produce a durable advantage on achievement tests, which fades by third grade in the national randomized evaluation [1] and turns negative by sixth grade in Tennessee's [3]. Adult outcomes — earnings, health, arrests — are known almost entirely from two small demonstration programs of the 1960s and 1970s [4][5], whose participants faced a counterfactual of no organized care that few children face today. The strongest opposing view is that Tennessee shows a modern statewide program can leave children measurably worse off rather than merely no better; that is a genuine result and not one the other studies refute, so the honest form of the answer is that the evidence discriminates on program quality rather than on preschool as such.

## Key findings

- The national Head Start randomized evaluation found initial cognitive gains that were no longer statistically detectable by third grade [1].
- Tennessee's Voluntary Pre-K program, evaluated by lottery in oversubscribed sites, showed participants behind controls on achievement by third grade [2] and worse on both achievement and disciplinary infractions by sixth grade [3].
- The Perry Preschool Project — 123 low-income children in Ypsilanti, Michigan, randomized beginning in 1962 — reports higher earnings and fewer arrests at age 40 [4]; the Abecedarian project reports better adult cardiovascular and metabolic health [5].
- Boston's lottery-allocated pre-K produced no lasting test-score advantage but raised on-time high-school graduation, SAT-taking and college enrolment [6].

## The strongest counterargument

The case for durable benefit does not depend on test scores at all, and its strongest modern form is Boston's. Gray-Lobe, Pathak and Walters [6] exploit the district's admissions lottery, follow applicants from the 1997-2003 cohorts into their twenties, and find no persistent advantage on standardized tests alongside higher rates of on-time high-school graduation and college enrolment. If the mechanism runs through school engagement rather than through measured skill, then achievement-test fade-out is the wrong place to look for the effect, and every fade-out finding above is compatible with a program that works.

Two things stop that from settling the question. Boston's program is unusually well resourced and staffed at public-school pay scales, so it is not representative of state programs generally; and Deming [7], who finds long-run gains of a similar shape using sibling comparisons within Head Start families, is working with a design that cannot fully rule out family-level differences in which sibling was enrolled. The two agree in direction, which is why the answer above concedes attainment effects while declining to generalize them from Boston to programs run on half its budget.

## How far the modern evaluations reach

The Head Start Impact Study randomly assigned roughly 5,000 applicants across a national sample of programs and followed them to the end of third grade [1]. It is the only national randomized evidence there is, and its finding is the origin of the fade-out framing: measurable cognitive advantages at the end of the pre-K year, largely gone three years later.

Tennessee's evaluation is the strongest modern design outside Boston, because places in oversubscribed sites were allocated by lottery and the comparison therefore rests on randomization rather than on statistical adjustment. Lipsey, Farran and Durkin [2] report the third-grade results, with participants behind controls on achievement, and Durkin and colleagues [3] extend the same cohort to sixth grade, where both the achievement gap and the rate of disciplinary infractions run against the pre-K group.

Durkin and colleagues [3] also tracked that cohort through twelfth grade and report that the sixth-grade deficit closes and then reverses, with pre-K participants more likely to graduate on time and less likely to be chronically absent in their final two years. That is the only long-run randomized estimate available for a statewide program, and it is the single strongest reason to treat the fade-out results as a description of the middle years rather than of the outcome.

## What the demonstration programs establish

Perry randomized 123 low-income children in Ypsilanti, Michigan into a two-year preschool program beginning in 1962 and has followed them ever since; at age 40 the treatment group reported higher earnings and fewer arrests than the control group [4]. Heckman and colleagues [8] put the annual social rate of return at roughly 7 to 10 percent, a range whose width comes mostly from the discount rate and from how the small sample is handled.

Abecedarian, a North Carolina program beginning in infancy, reports better cardiovascular and metabolic health in the treated group in their mid-thirties [5]. Both programs were small, intensive, and run against a counterfactual of no organized care at all. Neither licenses a claim about what a modern state program competing against widely available childcare would do, which is the limitation the whole adult-outcomes literature inherits.
